concepts.label: Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Sectors
concepts.cardText: When we produce a good by exploiting natural resources, such as cotton, milk or minerals, it is an activity of the primary sector, also called agriculture and related sector, because it forms the base for all other products. The secondary sector changes natural products into other forms through manufacturing, like cotton into cloth or sugarcane into sugar; it is also called the industrial sector. The tertiary sector does not produce a good but supports production: transport, storage, communication, banking and trade. Since these generate services, it is also called the service sector.
concepts.hint: Does the activity use nature directly, make something in a factory or workshop, or provide a service?
concepts.probe: Explain the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary sectors with examples.
concepts.causeChain: Primary sector exploits natural resources (base for all products) -> secondary sector manufactures natural products into other forms -> tertiary sector supports both with services such as transport, storage and banking

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that the primary sector is called primary because it forms the base for the products that the secondary sector later makes.

keyPoints.text: When we produce a good by exploiting natural resources, it is an activity of the primary sector. Why primary? This is because it forms the base for all other products that we subsequently make. Since most of the natural products we get are from agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, this sector is also called agriculture and related sector.
keyPoints.followUp: What kind of activities belong to the primary sector, and why is it called 'primary'?

checks.criterion: Defines the primary sector as producing goods by exploiting natural resources (for example agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry or minerals).

keyPoints.text: The secondary sector covers activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through ways of manufacturing that we associate with industrial activity. Using cotton fibre we spin yarn and weave cloth; using sugarcane we make sugar or gur. Since this sector gradually became associated with different kinds of industries, it is also called the industrial sector.
keyPoints.followUp: What happens to natural products in the secondary sector? Give an example.

requiredEvidence: natural products are changed into other forms

checks.criterion: Defines the secondary sector as changing natural products into other forms through manufacturing (for example cotton into cloth, sugarcane into sugar).

keyPoints.text: The tertiary sector covers activities that help in the development of the primary and secondary sectors. These activities, by themselves, do not produce a good but they are an aid or a support for the production process. Transport, storage, communication, banking, trade are some examples. Since these activities generate services rather than goods, the tertiary sector is also called the service sector. It also includes essential services like teachers, doctors, washermen, barbers, lawyers, and new IT-based services.
keyPoints.followUp: How is the tertiary sector different from the other two? Give some examples.

checks.criterion: Defines the tertiary (service) sector as activities that do not produce a good but support production, such as transport, storage, communication, banking or trade.
Mentions that the service sector also includes essential services like teachers, doctors, barbers or lawyers, or new IT-based services.

concepts.label: Interdependence of the Three Sectors
concepts.cardText: Economic activities are grouped into three sectors, but they are highly interdependent. If farmers refuse to sell sugarcane to a sugar mill, the mill will have to shut down: industry depends on the primary sector. If the price of fertilisers or pumpsets goes up, farmers' costs rise: agriculture depends on industry. If transporters strike, food becomes scarce in cities and farmers cannot sell their products: both depend on services.

concepts.causeChain: Mills need farm produce; farmers need fertilisers and pumpsets; both need transport and trade -> a problem in one sector affects the others -> the sectors are highly interdependent

keyPoints.text: Economic activities, though grouped into three different categories, are highly interdependent.

checks.criterion: States that the three sectors, though grouped separately, are highly interdependent.

If the price of fertilisers or pumpsets goes up, the cost of cultivation rises and farmers' profits fall. If transporters strike and lorries refuse to take vegetables and milk from rural areas, food becomes scarce in urban areas and farmers cannot sell their products.

concepts.label: Final Goods, Intermediate Goods and GDP
concepts.cardText: To add up production, economists use the values of goods and services, not their numbers. Only final goods and services, those that reach consumers, are counted. Intermediate goods, like wheat and flour used to make biscuits, are used up in producing final goods, and the value of the final good already includes them. Counting them separately would count the same things several times. The sum of production in the three sectors is the Gross Domestic Product (GDP): the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. It shows how big the economy is.
concepts.hint: If you count the wheat, the flour and the biscuits, how many times have you counted the wheat?
concepts.probe: What is GDP, and why are only final goods and services counted?
concepts.causeChain: Final goods already include the value of intermediate goods -> counting intermediate goods separately would count the same value several times -> only final goods and services are counted -> their total is GDP

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that because the value of final goods already includes intermediate goods, counting intermediate goods separately would count the same value more than once.

keyPoints.text: To get around the problem of adding up so many goods and services, economists suggest that the values of goods and services should be used rather than adding up the actual numbers. For example, 10,000 kgs of wheat sold at Rs 20 per kg has a value of Rs 2,00,000.

requiredEvidence: rather than adding up the actual numbers

checks.criterion: Explains that production is measured by adding the values of goods and services, not their actual numbers.

keyPoints.text: It makes sense only to include the final goods and services, which reach the consumers. Intermediate goods, like wheat and wheat flour used for biscuits, are used up in producing final goods and services. The value of final goods already includes the value of all the intermediate goods used in making them, so counting the value of the flour and wheat separately would count the same things a number of times.

checks.criterion: States that only final goods and services (those that reach consumers) are counted.
Explains that intermediate goods are used up in producing final goods, and the value of final goods already includes them.

keyPoints.text: The value of final goods and services produced in each sector during a particular year provides the total production of the sector for that year. The sum of production in the different sectors gives the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of a country. It is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. GDP shows how big the economy is.

checks.criterion: Defines GDP as the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.

Recently the Indian Government began to bring out the contribution of the three sectors towards Gross Value Added (GVA), which measures their contribution after adjusting for taxes and subsidies.

checks.criterion: Mentions that GDP in India is measured by a central government ministry with the help of state departments.

concepts.label: Historical Change in Sectors
concepts.cardText: In now-developed countries, the primary sector was most important at the initial stages of development. As farming improved, agriculture produced much more food, so many people took up crafts, trade and other activities. Over more than a hundred years, new methods of manufacturing brought factories, and the secondary sector became the most important in production and employment. In the past 100 years, there has been a further shift from secondary to tertiary in developed countries: the service sector is now the most important in total production and employs most working people.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects new methods of manufacturing and expanding factories to the shift of importance from the primary to the secondary sector.

keyPoints.text: From the histories of many now developed countries, at initial stages of development, primary sector was the most important sector of economic activity. As the methods of farming changed and agriculture began to prosper, it produced much more food than before, and many people could take up other activities.

requiredEvidence: most important in total production and employment

checks.criterion: States that with new methods of manufacturing and expanding factories, the secondary sector became the most important in production and employment.

concepts.label: Rising Importance of the Tertiary Sector
concepts.cardText: Between 1977-78 and 2017-18, production rose in all three sectors but most in the tertiary sector, which became India's largest producing sector. Reasons: basic services like hospitals, schools, police, courts, transport and banks are needed, and the government provides them; development of agriculture and industry raises demand for transport, trade and storage; as incomes rise, people demand services like eating out, tourism and private schools; and new ICT-based services have grown rapidly. But not all of the service sector is growing: many small shopkeepers, repair persons and transport persons barely earn a living.
concepts.hint: Think of basic services, support for other sectors, rising incomes and information technology.
concepts.probe: Why is the tertiary sector becoming so important in India? Is all of it growing equally?
concepts.causeChain: Basic services needed + growth of agriculture and industry + rising incomes + new ICT services -> tertiary production grows most -> largest producing sector; but only a part of it (skilled services) is growing

causeLinks.criterion: Connects reasons such as rising incomes or growth of agriculture and industry to the tertiary sector becoming India's largest producing sector.

keyPoints.text: Over the forty years between 1977-78 and 2017-18, while production in all the three sectors has increased, it has increased the most in the tertiary sector. As a result, in 2017-18, the tertiary sector has emerged as the largest producing sector in India replacing the primary sector.
keyPoints.followUp: Which sector's production grew the most in India between 1977-78 and 2017-18?

requiredEvidence: increased the most in the tertiary sector

checks.criterion: States that production rose most in the tertiary sector, which became India's largest producing sector, replacing the primary sector.

keyPoints.text: Reasons: first, basic services such as hospitals, educational institutions, post and telegraph, police stations, courts, municipal corporations, defence, transport, banks and insurance are required, and in a developing country the government has to provide them. Second, development of agriculture and industry leads to demand for services such as transport, trade and storage. Third, as income levels rise, people demand many more services like eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals and private schools. Fourth, new services based on information and communication technology have become important and essential.

At the other end, a very large number of workers, such as small shopkeepers, repair persons and transport persons, barely manage to earn a living because no alternative opportunities for work are available. Only a part of this sector is growing in importance.

concepts.label: Where Are Most People Employed?
concepts.cardText: The share of the three sectors in GVA has changed, but a similar shift has not taken place in employment: the primary sector continues to be the largest employer. Not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors. Industrial output rose more than nine times but industrial employment only about three times; service production rose 14 times but service employment only about five times. So more than half of India's workers are in the primary sector, mainly agriculture, producing only about one sixth of the GVA.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects too few jobs being created in the secondary and tertiary sectors to the primary sector remaining the largest employer.

While production in the service sector rose by 14 times, employment in the service sector rose around five times.

concepts.label: Underemployment and Disguised Unemployment
concepts.cardText: There are more people in agriculture than necessary, so even if a few move out, production is not affected: agricultural workers are underemployed. Laxmi's family of five works on two hectares of unirrigated land; everyone works, but no one is fully employed. People apparently work but all work less than their potential. This hidden underemployment, unlike someone clearly without a job, is called disguised unemployment. If two members move to a factory, the farm produces as much and family income rises. It also exists in cities, among casual workers like painters, plumbers and repair persons.
concepts.hint: If two of Laxmi's five family members leave the farm, does the harvest fall?
concepts.probe: What is disguised unemployment? Explain with an example from rural and urban areas.
concepts.causeChain: More people in agriculture than necessary -> labour effort divided, no one fully employed -> people work below their potential (hidden) -> disguised unemployment -> removing workers does not reduce production

causeLinks.criterion: Connects there being more people in agriculture than necessary to production not falling when some move out, which is why the unemployment is disguised.

keyPoints.text: There are more people in agriculture than is necessary. So, even if you move a few people out, production will not be affected. In other words, workers in the agricultural sector are underemployed.

requiredEvidence: more people in agriculture than is necessary

checks.criterion: Explains that there are more people in agriculture than necessary, so moving some out would not affect production.

keyPoints.text: Laxmi owns about two hectares of unirrigated land; all five members of her family work on it throughout the year because they have nowhere else to go. Everyone is working, but their labour effort gets divided and no one is fully employed. This is underemployment, where people are apparently working but all of them are made to work less than their potential. This underemployment is hidden, in contrast to someone who clearly has no job, so it is also called disguised unemployment.

concepts.label: Ways to Create More Employment
concepts.cardText: A well, dam or canals let farmers like Laxmi irrigate land and grow a second crop, creating work within agriculture itself. Investment in transport, storage and rural roads lets farmers sell more, creating jobs in transport and trade. Cheap agricultural credit from banks helps farmers buy seeds and inputs. Industries and services in semi-rural areas, like a dal mill, cold storage, honey collection centres and food processing, can employ many people. A study estimates nearly 20 lakh jobs could be created in education alone, and many more in health and tourism.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects providing irrigation (a well, dam or canals) to farmers growing a second crop and more employment within agriculture.

keyPoints.text: The government can spend some money or banks can provide a loan to construct a well for Laxmi's family to irrigate the land. She can then take a second crop, wheat, during the rabi season, employing two more family members. If a new dam is constructed and canals are dug to irrigate many such farms, this could lead to a lot of employment generation within the agricultural sector itself, reducing the problem of underemployment.

requiredEvidence: employment generation within the agricultural sector

keyPoints.text: If the government invests in transportation and storage of crops, or makes better rural roads so that mini-trucks reach everywhere, farmers can grow and sell more, providing productive employment also to those in transport or trade. Along with water, cheap agricultural credit from banks at a reasonable rate of interest is needed so farmers can buy seeds, fertilisers, equipment and pumpsets.

checks.criterion: Suggests investing in transport, storage or rural roads so farmers can sell their crops, creating jobs in transport and trade.

keyPoints.text: Another way is to identify, promote and locate industries and services in semi-rural areas where a large number of people may be employed: a dal mill to process pulses, a cold storage for potatoes and onions, honey collection centres near forests, and industries that process vegetables and agricultural produce.

checks.criterion: Suggests locating industries and services in semi-rural areas, such as a dal mill, cold storage, honey collection centres or food processing units.

concepts.label: Right to Work: MGNREGA
concepts.cardText: Long-term measures take time, so the Union Government made a law implementing the Right to Work in about 625 districts: the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA). It guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year to all who are able and in need of work in rural areas; if the government failed, it would give unemployment allowances. Work that would help increase production from land was given preference. In 2025, the Act was replaced by Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Viksit Bharat-G RAM G 2025).

concepts.causeChain: Long-term measures take time -> quick measure needed -> law guarantees 100 days of rural employment a year -> unemployment allowance if work is not provided -> 'Right to Work'

keyPoints.text: Under MGNREGA 2005, all those who are able to, and are in need of, work in rural areas were guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year by the government. If the government fails in its duty to provide employment, it would give unemployment allowances to the people.
keyPoints.followUp: What does MGNREGA promise rural people, and what happens if the government cannot keep the promise?

checks.criterion: States that MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed 100 days of employment a year to those able and in need of work in rural areas.

topics.title: Division of sectors as organised and unorganised

concepts.label: Organised and Unorganised Sectors
concepts.cardText: Kanta works in an office with regular hours, a monthly salary, provident fund, medical allowances, paid holidays and an appointment letter: the organised sector. Organised sector enterprises have regular terms of employment, are registered by the government and follow laws like the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act. Workers get job security, fixed hours, overtime, paid leave, provident fund, gratuity and pensions. Kamal, a daily wage worker in a grocery shop, has no leave, no allowances, no appointment letter and can be asked to leave anytime: the unorganised sector of small, scattered units largely outside government control, where rules are not followed.

concepts.label: Protecting Workers in the Unorganised Sector
concepts.cardText: Organised sector jobs are most sought-after, but they have been expanding very slowly, and some organised enterprises operate in the unorganised sector to evade taxes and labour laws. Since the 1990s, many workers have lost organised sector jobs. So workers in the unorganised sector need protection and support. In rural areas they are landless labourers, small and marginal farmers (nearly 80 per cent of rural households), sharecroppers and artisans; in urban areas, workers in small-scale industry, casual workers, street vendors, head load workers and rag pickers. Most workers from scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities are in this sector and also face social discrimination.

Nearly 80 per cent of rural households are small and marginal farmers, who need timely seeds, inputs, credit, storage and marketing outlets. In urban areas, it comprises workers in small-scale industry, casual workers in construction, trade and transport, street vendors, head load workers, garment makers and rag pickers.

topics.title: Sectors in terms of ownership: public and private sectors

concepts.label: Public and Private Sectors
concepts.cardText: Sectors can also be classified by who owns assets and is responsible for delivering services. In the public sector, the government owns most of the assets and provides all the services, like the Railways or the post office. In the private sector, ownership of assets and delivery of services is in the hands of private individuals or companies, like TISCO or RIL. Private sector activities are guided by the motive to earn profits; the purpose of the public sector is not just to earn profits. Governments raise money through taxes to meet the expenses of their services.

Railways or post office are public sector; companies like TISCO or RIL are privately owned.

concepts.label: Why the Government Spends on Public Activities
concepts.cardText: Some things society needs will not be provided by the private sector at a reasonable cost: roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity and irrigation dams need large sums of money, and collecting payment from thousands of users is hard. The government also supports some activities: it supplies electricity at rates small-scale industries can afford, and buys wheat and rice from farmers at a 'fair price' and sells them cheaper through ration shops, supporting both farmers and consumers. Health and education for all, safe drinking water, housing and nutrition, and care of the poorest regions are its primary responsibility.

keyPoints.text: There are several things needed by society as a whole which the private sector will not provide at a reasonable cost. Some need spending large sums of money, beyond the capacity of the private sector, and collecting money from thousands of users is not easy. Examples are construction of roads, bridges, railways, harbours, generating electricity, providing irrigation through dams. Governments undertake such heavy spending and ensure these facilities are available for everyone.

keyPoints.text: A large number of activities are the primary responsibility of the government. Government must also attend to safe drinking water, housing for the poor, food and nutrition, and the poorest regions.
